title: A Card to Send
sub: Grades 1–2 · Christmas Card Maker · The first Christmas card
objective: Students will hear how Henry Cole, with too much Christmas mail to answer, had the first Christmas card made in 1843. They will find the symbols Victorian cards made famous — robins, holly and snowy scenes — and design a card of their own, with a picture, a border and a greeting, for someone they care about.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A card is a small picture with a big job: it tells someone far away that you are thinking of them. The Victorians sent the very first Christmas cards, and we still send them today.

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
The *Christmas Card Maker* on a screen, if you have one
Crayons or colored pencils, and the differentiated handouts
questions: Which symbols can you find on these cards?
Why do you think robins, holly and snow became Christmas symbols?
Henry Cole’s card showed people giving to others. Why might he choose that?
Who would you send a card to, and what would you put on it?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in the *Christmas Card Maker*, children choose a picture, a border and a paper, write their greeting inside, then print and fold their card. The first card’s greeting is one of the choices.
**In Dickens’ Christmas Parlour,** find the Christmas cards standing along the mantelpiece.

steps.title: A robin in the snow
script: Show the robin card front. Give the class a quiet minute to look. *“What do you see?”* A robin, a snowy branch, holly with red berries. Then: *“Why would someone put a robin on a Christmas card?”* Take ideas. *“Today you will find out who sent the very first Christmas card — and then you will make one.”*

screen.alt: A robin on a snowy branch of holly with red berries
screen.caption: A card front in the Christmas Card Maker

steps.purpose: Look closely at a card front, and wonder about its picture, before any story.
students: Why would someone put a robin on a Christmas card?

steps.title: Too much mail
script: Tell the story. In 1843, a man named Henry Cole had so much Christmas mail piling up that he could not answer it all. He asked his friend, the artist John Callcott Horsley, to design a card he could send instead. The card showed three generations of the Cole family raising a toast, with scenes of giving to people in need around it, and the greeting *“A merry Christmas and a Happy New Year”*. A thousand copies were printed. Ask: *“Why was one card, printed many times, a clever idea?”*

screen.question: Henry Cole had too much Christmas mail. What could he do?

steps.purpose: Hear the true story of the first Christmas card as a problem and its clever answer.
students: What would you do with a pile of letters to answer?

steps.title: Find the symbols
script: Show the four card fronts from the *Christmas Card Maker*. Explain that they are new pictures, made for the exhibition in the style of Victorian cards. Victorian cards made robins, holly, snowy scenes and Father Christmas into the symbols of the season — one card even shows Father Christmas riding a bicycle! Let children come up and point to each symbol.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Circle the robin, the holly and the snowy church; finish Henry Cole’s story from a word bank; draw a card front; copy the first card’s greeting.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Name the symbol on each card; explain in a sentence why Henry Cole had a card made; design a front and write the inside, with *To* and *From*.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Choose a card to send and say why; explain why a printed card saved time; design a card that helps someone feel cared for.

steps.purpose: Find the symbols, retell the story and design a card, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Every level ends with a card of your own.

steps.title: Share your card
script: Students hold up their cards. Partners tell each other: *who is it for, and why that picture?* Ask two or three to share with the class.

screen.question: Hold up your card. Tell a partner who it is for, and why you chose your picture.

steps.purpose: Say who a card is for, as the first card’s greeting did.
students: Why did you choose your picture?

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back from the screen: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. For the last, ask a Red Level student to explain.
